brief: A field-guide plate shows a dozen house keys as if they were species. Each lies at the same angle in tidy staggered rows on muted grey-green tinted paper, with faint numerals beside each. Use opaque gouache-like marker and fine coloured pencil: worn brass, nickel silver, a rust-flecked iron skeleton key, a plastic-headed key in faded teal. Show the distinguishing marks of each, such as bitting profiles, stamped maker's lettering, patina in the grooves and pocket-scratches. Every key casts the same small soft shadow to the lower right. The tone is calm and taxonomic, and the variety within the set rewards close comparison.

Three cut lemons glisten against a field of gold tesserae, built from thousands of small square marker dabs. Each tile is slightly tilted, with ochre, amber, umber and pale gold variations, and dark grout lines between them. The lemons are made of smaller, tighter tesserae that follow their curvature, rendering hyperreal juice beads, translucent segment walls, a pip and the pitted rind. A solitary bay leaf rests in deep green glass tiles. The flat gold glimmers unevenly, while the fruit glows with almost devotional intensity.

Look straight down on a patisserie display of macarons arranged in long single-colour rows, like Dutch bulb fields seen from a plane. Stripes of pistachio, raspberry, violet, lemon, coffee and pale rose run diagonally across the sheet and are cut by tracks of empty tray. Use clean watercolour fills for each band, then sharpen every shell: the ruffled feet, the faint cracks, the filling bulging out, crumbs on the parchment liner. Give each macaron a low soft shadow. The overall image is pattern-dominant, joyful and immaculately ordered.

A torn sourdough boule is rendered entirely as a burin engraving in sepia-black fine pen on warm cream laid paper. Nothing is filled. The scorched ear, the floured blistered crust and the open crumb are all made from tapering swelling lines, cross-hatching laid at shifting angles and dot-and-lozenge stipple in the deepest alveoli. The line work follows the bread's curvature like contour lines on a globe. The tear exposes glossy gelatinised crumb, which is read through tighter, darker hatching beside untouched paper highlights. Place the loaf off-centre on a bare linen fold that is engraved in long parallel strokes. The mood is austere, archival and obsessively patient.

A half-eaten birthday cake sits on a cluttered kitchen table seconds after the candles were blown out, captured as if handheld with no added light. The framing is tilted and crops off the plate edge. Grey window daylight leaks from one side, and the candle smoke drifts in soft charcoal smears. Hyperreal detail survives in graphite and coloured pencil: smeared buttercream, a fork stuck in sponge, wax drips, a child's sticky fingerprint on the foil. A slight motion blur drags the foreground, and pencil grain over everything mimics film. The tone is warm, unglamorous and intimate.

Treat a sticky cinnamon roll as a specimen on a nineteenth-century conchology plate. Arrange four views in a tidy grid on yellowed paper: the top spiral, the underside caramel base, a vertical cross-section, and an unrolled length of dough. Each view gets a tiny pencilled reference numeral. Draw graphite underlayers, then glaze them with transparent watercolour in burnt umber, cassia brown and translucent honey. Cream-cheese icing is left as reserved paper and edged with cool grey pencil. Add sharp cast shadows and a gloss on the sugar crust. The cool, classifying calm of the layout contrasts with the gooey subject.

A splitting maul is buried in a scarred oak chopping block, rendered as a stark German Expressionist woodcut pushed to hyperreal fidelity. Use only dense black ink and white paper. The forms are carved out by angular gouges, jagged parallel strokes and splintered chisel marks that follow real grain, growth rings and the axe's hammered steel. Rough bark is chunky crosshatch, and the bright bevelled edge is a single raw white slash. The view tilts upward from a low angle with harsh raking light and deep chiaroscuro. Wood chips scatter as sharp white shards, and the mood is tense and physical.

A bunch of radishes lies diagonally across a glossy white surface, their greens splayed like serrated saz leaves. Use the Iznik palette strictly: raised tomato-bole red for the roots, turquoise and deep cobalt in the leaf shadows, sage green, and fine black outlines. Lay each colour as dense flat marker passages, then model it toward full hyperreal volume: soil grit in the root hairs, the waxy bloom on the skin, torn leaf veins. Thin white highlights mimic the sheen of fritware glaze across the whole image, as if the radishes were alive beneath a glassy coat.

A small espresso cup on its saucer sits low on a stark, mid-grey ground. Above it, rising heat is rendered as schlieren imaging: knife-edged twisting plumes in silver, graphite and black, sharply light on one side and dark on the other, like a physics photograph. The cup itself is precise hyperreal porcelain with a tiger-striped crema and a reflected window. Smudged charcoal gradients and fine spray build the turbulence, and hard graphite edges catch the shear lines. It is monochrome, scientific and theatrical, and the invisible air becomes the real subject.

A single broccoli floret is staged like a prized bonsai on a rough black slate slab. Its stalk twists like a trunk and its florets are pruned into cloud pads. Low raking studio light from the left throws the bud clusters into granular, sculptural relief. The colours run from bluish jade through chartreuse to a pale celery-white trunk with fibrous striations. Dense, burnished coloured pencil gives the slate its chalky bloom. A thread of copper wire coils round one branch. The composition is off-centre with generous dark space, contemplative and faintly comic.

A chipped enamel camping mug, shown in tight three-quarter view on a raw plank, is built the way pysanky dyes an egg. Colour climbs in stages from chrome yellow to marigold to madder red and finally a glossy aubergine-black. Fine white resist lines are left untouched, and these double as the mug's razor specular highlights and the hairline edges of each chip. Saturated alcohol-marker layers build up into an enamel gloss. The chipped spots expose blue-black steel with tiny rust halos. The look is folk-bright yet photographically exact.

A tied bundle of celery stalks lies horizontally across a long, low format. The stalks are dissected by fine black pen lines into rectilinear facets, like Prairie School leaded glass. Each facet is a translucent ink fill in chartreuse, amber, olive, buff or iridescent milky white. Within each facet the hyperreal detail persists: stringy ribs, a water bead, the bruised cut end. Straight lines and repeated horizontals echo Wright's glass, and a narrow border band of squares runs along the bottom. The light is warm and filtered, and the whole is architectural and calm.

A hand slowly entering still bathwater, viewed from directly above. Its fingertips are rendered hyperreal in coloured pencil: wrinkled skin, a chipped nail and trapped air beads. Outward from the point of entry spread dense concentric rings, drawn as continuous fine wavering watercolour lines in indigo, soft carbon grey and a thin rust red. They distort and drift like floating-ink marbling, bending where the tiles beneath refract. The composition is full-bleed with no empty margins. It feels meditative, rippling and exact.

The view is a dizzying worm's-eye looking straight up as a cluster of helium balloons escapes into a summer sky. In the foreground, a foreshortened child's hand has just let go, and curling ribbons spiral up toward the vanishing point. The balloons are glossy latex in cadmium red, ultramarine and lemon, each holding a warped window reflection. The sky deepens from cerulean at the edges to pale haze at the centre, like a painted Baroque ceiling opening to heaven. Layered watercolour sits under crisp marker highlights. It is vertiginous, celebratory and illusionistic.

A single ripe persimmon sits on a deep black lacquered tray and is mirrored in its liquid surface. The palette is strictly vermilion, cinnabar and black, with one ochre accent on the calyx. The fruit's skin is hyperreal: a faint waxy bloom, a tiny bruise and a crisp window reflection. Its reflection breaks into flowing cloud-scroll streaks that echo Han lacquer ornament. Dense opaque marker is layered for a deep gloss, with sharp edges and almost no gradient in the black. It is ceremonial, symmetrical-leaning and silent.

An extreme crop of a cheetah's flank fills the whole sheet edge to edge, with no animal outline. The spots behave like a reaction-diffusion field, merging and splitting into labyrinthine clusters across the curve of the ribs. Thousands of directional fur strokes follow a flowing field in warm ochre, raw sienna and cream. The spots are dense black-brown pen stippling with soft, bleeding edges where the hair parts. Raking side light picks out each hair tip. It is obsessive, tactile and slightly hypnotic.

A single strawberry is rendered at postage-stamp intimacy, inside a perforated white border with a tiny denomination numeral and a small printed country name. The berry is built from dense line-engraving cross-hatch in fine pen, swelling and thinning across the form, with seeds as precise dots and a hairy calyx. One spot colour of carmine is printed slightly off-register beneath the black linework. A wavy black postmark cancellation slashes across one corner. The whole stamp sits slightly askew on cream envelope paper, giving collectable, miniature precision.

A hyperreal timber pier piling fills a tall, narrow vertical format, read like a tide chart turned to wood. Horizontal bands stack upward: slick black-green kelp at the base, then a crust of acorn barnacles, mussel-blue clusters, bleached grey grain, and dry silver-cracked wood at the top. Each high-water mark is a crisp ruled line of salt scum. Layered transparent watercolour glazes in viridian, burnt umber and Payne's grey carry the wetness, with sharp graphite detail on every barnacle plate and split in the grain. Flat, overcast light gives no drama, only patient, documentary measurement.

A split pomegranate in hyperreal detail, with ruby arils glistening, pith membranes torn and a single drip of juice. It is enthroned at the centre of a thangka-like structure of nested borders. Concentric bands of cloud scrolls, lotus petals and flame motifs surround it, filled with flat mineral colour: malachite green, lapis blue, cinnabar red and orpiment yellow. Fine gold pen outlines trace every motif. Paint the borders in dense, even watercolour fills with hairline detail, and model the fruit with deep glazes and crisp white highlights. The effect is devotional and ordered, with strict symmetry and tight brocade-like framing.

A ferry deck railing runs diagonally out of a white-on-white world. Behind it, a ghostly colourless fog bow arcs across the frame, with only the faintest blush of apricot on its outer edge and a cold violet-grey inside. The painted steel rail is rendered with total fidelity: chipped cream enamel, rust blooms, and beads of condensation hanging from the underside. The medium is soft, layered spray mist and powdery charcoal blending, so edges dissolve into fog everywhere except the rail, which stays knife-sharp in the near ground. It feels hushed, damp and almost blank.
